back: The lightest censure: a formal reproof by a court warning an offender of his guilt and danger.
The transfer of a judicial case, after judgment, to the next higher court. Only the party against whom the decision went may appeal.
A believer living away from his permanent home who joins a church without leaving his home church. He may not vote in congregational meetings or hold office.
A pastor elected by the congregation and a member of the Session. His relation to the church is determined by the congregation.
A pastor called by the Session with presbytery’s approval. He is not a member of the Session and his relation is determined by the Session.
Godly men and women appointed by a Session to help the deacons care for those in need. They are not officers and are not ordained.
The part of the Constitution containing the Form of Government, the Rules of Discipline and the Directory for Worship.
A communicant member who believes himself called to preach and submits himself to a presbytery’s care and guidance during his preparation.
A judgment of a court on an offender. The five censures are admonition, suspension from the sacraments, excommunication, suspension from office and deposition.
The written summons issued by order of a court calling an accused person or a witness to appear.
The standard under which a higher court may overturn a lower court’s finding of fact or its judgment on matters that turn on personal knowledge of the parties.
A body authorized to deliberate on and conclude the business referred to it, unlike a committee, which examines and reports.
A committee of the Assembly’s own commissioners through which business ordinarily reaches the floor.
A person who has professed faith in Christ, has been baptized and has been admitted by the Session to the Lord’s Table.
A written representation against an act or decision of a court, open to any communing member in good standing who is subject to that court.
Refusal to obey a citation, to plead, or otherwise to cooperate with lawful proceedings. It draws immediate suspension.
An assembly of presbyters exercising joint jurisdiction: a Session, a presbytery or the General Assembly.
An ordinary and perpetual officer whose work is sympathy and service, including the care of the needy and of church property, under the Session.
Suspension from office for a stated period, used when the offender has satisfied the court as to repentance but the honor of Christ still requires it.
The degrading of an officer from his office, which may or may not carry other censure with it.

key: t:Directory for the Worship of God
front: Directory for the Worship of God
back: The third part of the Book of Church Order. It is an approved guide, except that chapters 56, 57 and 58 and section 59-3 have full constitutional authority.
A recorded declaration by a member of the minority that his opinion differs from the court’s action, with reasons if he wishes.
The removal of office from a minister who lacks acceptance in the church, by two-thirds of presbytery, without a finding of guilt.
The officer, in two orders, who governs and oversees the church. Bishop, pastor, presbyter and teacher name one office, not grades.
The designation of a ruling elder or deacon released for age or infirmity, who may attend and speak at meetings but not vote.
Removal of a name from the roll as an act of pastoral discipline without process, after willful neglect and warning.
A teaching elder commissioned for a renewable term of twelve months where there are no PCA churches nearby or in foreign countries, with added powers by separate action of presbytery.
The cutting off of an offender from the communion of the church, used only for gross crime or heresy in one who is incorrigible and contumacious.
A declared difference with the Confession or Catechisms that a court judges may be allowed because it is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion.
The highest court, which represents all the churches in one body and is a permanent court meeting at least annually.
A heresy or immorality considered apart from any wrong to a particular person.
The designation of a minister who wishes to retire by reason of age. He keeps his membership in presbytery and may serve on committees or commissions.
Suspension from the sacraments or from office, without a set end, laid on an impenitent offender until he shows repentance.
The setting of an already ordained officer into a particular charge, without repeating ordination.
A trial period of at least one year, set and supervised by presbytery, in which a candidate’s gifts for ministry are tested.
The joint power of a court to judge. Each court has exclusive original jurisdiction over matters belonging to it, subject to review and control above.
The authority committed to church officers to shut the kingdom against the impenitent by the Word and censures and to open it to penitent sinners.
A man licensed by a presbytery to preach within its bounds. The license runs four years and may be renewed.
The character of all church power: courts serve and declare the law of Christ found in Scripture; they do not make laws that bind the conscience.
A congregation with no permanent governing body, supervised by others, whose goal is to be organized as a particular church.
The officer who presides in a court, with authority to preserve order and conduct business. The pastor moderates his Session by virtue of office.
A child of believers, a member of the church by covenant and birth, entitled to baptism, oversight, instruction and government.
A recorded declaration by a member of a court who had no right to vote on an appeal or complaint but differs from the decision.
Anything in the doctrine or practice of a professing member that is contrary to the Word of God, proved from Scripture as the Standards expound it.
The authoritative admission of a duly called man to office, with prayer and the laying on of hands, and only to a definite work.
The right first to hear and determine a case: presbytery for ministers, the Session for members, with narrow exceptions.
Ordinarily the request of a presbytery for action by the General Assembly on a specific matter.
The equal standing of elders in one office. Ruling elders have the same authority and eligibility in the courts as teaching elders.
A congregation of professing Christians with their children, associated for worship and godly living and submitting to the government of Christ’s kingdom.
A violation of God’s law considered as a wrong or injury to a particular person, which ordinarily requires private steps before prosecution.
Power exercised jointly by officers in courts, after the form of judgment.
Power exercised by officers severally, as in preaching, administering the sacraments, reproving, visiting and comforting.
The court made up of the teaching elders and churches within its bounds. When it meets as a court it comprises teaching elders and ruling elders elected by Sessions.
An offense known only to a few, as distinct from a public offense, which is notorious.
The representative of the Church in a case of process, either a voluntary prosecutor or one appointed by the court, and always a member of the court except in some Session cases.
A more solemn and formal declaration by a minority bearing testimony against what it deems an improper or erroneous action.
The committee elected by a congregation to seek and recommend a pastoral candidate.
The charges, answer, citations and returns, minutes and recordings that a lower court sends up. A higher court considers nothing outside it without consent.
A written application by a lower court asking a higher court for advice or for action on a matter still pending below.
The mode by which a higher court examines the records and proceedings of the court below and requires correction.
An elder, not a minister of the Word, furnished by Christ with gifts and commission to govern, with the same authority in the courts as a teaching elder.
The Assembly’s own operating rules. They are printed with the Book of Church Order but are not part of the Constitution.
The court of a particular church: the pastor, associate pastors and ruling elders, in which the church’s jurisdiction is lodged.
The teaching that the church’s power is exclusively spiritual and its courts have no jurisdiction in political or civil affairs. The phrase is not in the text; the doctrine is.
The Assembly’s commission of twenty-four elders to which all matters under the Rules of Discipline are committed, except the annual review of presbytery records.
The clerk elected by a court to record its transactions, preserve its records and grant extracts, which stand as evidence in every court.
A temporary relation between a church and a minister where no pastor can be secured, for no longer than a year at a time.
An elder specially gifted, called and trained to preach, who also administers the sacraments and holds his membership in presbytery.
The provision in the PC(USA) Book of Order holding congregational property in trust for that denomination. The PCA has no such clause.
All those throughout the world who profess the true religion, together with their children, in every age of redemptive history.

Three-fourths at all three steps

More than one witness, or one witness with corroborative evidence

Valid as testimony of good standing for one year

Not over thirty minutes a side, appellant opening and closing
